#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when your dependency graph turns into a cycle*
This scenario demonstrates how Maven handles a cycle between two published artifacts (A → B → A).

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Maven 3.9**; the behaviour shown applies to Maven 3.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA["lib-circle-a:1.0.0"]
    LibA --> LibB["lib-circle-b:1.0.0"]
    LibB --> LibA
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s10-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
A cycle (A depends on B, B depends on A) sends the resolver into an infinite loop or a stack overflow, or at least produces a warning.

#### ! Actual
The build succeeds, silently. Both artifacts are on the classpath and the tree simply stops where it would repeat itself.

#### ! Why
Maven's resolver keeps a record of the nodes already on the current path and does not descend into one it has seen. That is enough to terminate, so no error is raised and no warning is printed; the cycle is invisible unless you compare the tree with the libraries' POMs. Cycles between *modules of the same reactor build* are a different case: those fail immediately with "The projects in the reactor contain a cyclic reference", because Maven must order the modules to build them.

#### ! Fix
Refactor to break the cycle, typically by extracting the shared part into a third library both can depend on. Nothing in the POM can fix a cycle between artifacts you do not publish; you can only avoid consuming them.

#### ! Risk
* LOW A cycle between two artifacts released in lockstep by the same team.
* MEDIUM A cycle you consume from a third party: upgrading either half means upgrading both.
* HIGH A cycle inside your own modules. The build will refuse it, and the fix is architectural.

#### ! Control
Avoid cycles. They are a design smell.

#### ! Check

**Fast check:**

```bash
mvn dependency:tree
```

**What to look for:**
`lib-circle-a` → `lib-circle-b`, with no second `lib-circle-a` beneath it and no warning. That absence is the only clue.

**Conclusion:**
Circular dependencies between published artifacts resolve silently; they still indicate a design problem.

#### ! Scales
Cycles make it impossible to build modules in a linear order, forcing them to be built together or released in lockstep.

#### ! Takeaway
Maven breaks artifact cycles without telling you and refuses reactor cycles outright. Both are the same architectural problem; only one of them is loud.

#### ! Wild
The cycle most teams actually meet is the loud one. A multi-module build has `core` and `util`; `core` depends on `util`. Someone writing a test in `util` wants a helper from `core`, adds a `test`-scoped dependency, and the next `mvn install` from the root stops with "The projects in the reactor contain a cyclic reference". Scope does not matter to the reactor: a dependency is an edge, and the modules can no longer be ordered. The fix is always the same, move the shared piece into a third module, and it is always more work than the one-line dependency that caused it.
